transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-04-01 13:30 PDT
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (CSM), Mike (Mosaic CTO), Sara (Lead ML), Tom (Infra), Lina (Product)

Summary (auto): Week-5 wrap of session coalescing/prefix reuse pilot. We reviewed hit-rate numbers, changes pushed mid-week to coalescing window, and agreed on an instrumentation + steady-state run. Action items and benchmark schedule confirmed.

[00:00] Alex: alright everyone thanks for joining, uh I know we have a packed agenda so we'll go quick. quick roll call?
[00:08] Mike: mike here.
[00:09] Sara: sara.
[00:10] Tom: tom.
[00:11] Lina: lina.
[00:12] Alex: and alex, priya and jordan on our side. cool. so the goal today is to review week five numbers after we enabled session coalescing and the adjusted eviction policy.
[00:26] Priya: yeah I can start, I pulled the telemetry. just to be clear coalescing here means we group concurrent session prefixes into a shared cache context, not sticky affinity. that reduced redundant kv insertions in our runs.
[00:42] Sara: can you unpack that a little? when you say group, does that mean you merge user sessions or just merge identical prefix keys?
[00:49] Priya: mosty the latter, we canonicalize tokenized prefixes and then canonical keys are deduped so the cache entry is shared. So two sessions with the same recent prompt prefix hit the same kv entry. we experimented with a 30s coalesce window, then 90s in a later patch.
[01:07] Tom: i think we saw less network chatter which helps our infra costs. but curious about eviction - we had some misses which caused regen.
[01:15] Priya: right; eviction was tuned from LRU-like to time-decay with a bias toward longer-lived prefixes. that improved hit retention for repeated assistance flows.
[01:23] Alex: key numbers: overall kv/prefix hit-rate rose from about 18% baseline to 28% with 30s window and to ~33% with 90s in daytime traffic. token-level savings translated to approx 12-15% CPU/token cost reduction in our estimates.
[01:40] Mike: 33% sounds good but our primary concern is tail latency. any increase in 99th?
[01:46] Priya: short answer, we saw no significant 99th degradation in our internal sampling at low QPS. however in a burst test we observed a few outliers when eviction chased under memory pressure — those were up to +120ms on 99th. we suspect network serialization during cache miss paths aggravated it.
[02:07] Sara: hmm ok. what's the miss breakdown — prompt rewrite vs prefix mismatch vs kv formatting?
[02:13] Priya: it's about 45% true misses (new prefix), 30% near-match mismatch (tokenization differences), 25% eviction-induced misses. we'll need to address tokenization normalization and prefix coalescing heuristics.
[02:27] Alex: quick qual question - what fraction of your traffic are multi-turn support conversations vs one-shots?
[02:33] Sara: roughly 60% multi-turn, those are the ones that should benefit most. product side is about 30% one-shots like simple lookups.
[02:39] Alex: good, that aligns. Lina, from product perspective, is 90s coalesce window acceptable? any privacy concerns?
[02:47] Lina: privacy team flagged retention in cache but it's encrypted and we can token redaction. main ask is a clear TTL and ability to scrub on demand.
[02:55] Alex: Redwood supports customer-managed KMS and option to zero-out cache entries via API. we'll include that in the runbook.
[03:03] Mike: SOC2 and audit logs are necessary for compliance signoff. can you provide audit trail for cache evictions and who triggered scrubs?
[03:11] Jordan: yes we emit audit events to the control plane; we'll share the schema. Priya will also add a debug flag for more detailed eviction traces.
[03:19] Priya: on the tokenization mismatch, one workaround is to run lightweight normalizer on the client side (lowercase, strip punctuation) before constructing prefix keys. that reduced near-match misses by about 12% in our lab.
[03:33] Tom: would that be safe for medical contexts? we worry about meaning changes.
[03:38] Priya: good call — we'll scope normalizer to non-PII tokens and avoid semantic transforms. also we can send original prompt in logs but use normalized key for caching only.
[03:48] Sara: numbers look promising. do you have per-route breakdown? the support flow had 42% hit-rate, the clinical triage flow only 18%.
[03:57] Alex: yes we sliced by route. product/helpdesk saw biggest gains because of repeat phrasing and templates. clinical triage tends to have more variability; we'll try prefix-length heuristics there.
[04:08] Mike: what's the plan to validate in our staging where traffic shape is closer to prod?
[04:13] Priya: propose a steady-state run: enable coalescing 90s, run traffic generator against staging for 2 hours at x% of prod QPS, capture token-level hit-rate, 95/99 latencies, and CPU/GPU utilization. we recommend a cold start warmup period of 15 minutes.
[04:29] Sara: ok, we can do that wk of 4/8. Tom will provision a test subnet for redwood instances.
[04:36] Tom: noted, i will open the firewall rules and provide temporary AWS role with least privilege.
[04:41] Alex: on instrumentation, priya to share small benchmark script and exact metrics names (we saw some confusion with metric prefix redwood.cache.* vs redwood.kv.*).
[04:52] Priya: yes, i'll include the tag mapping and a Grafana dashboard template.
[04:58] Mike: also can you show the cost delta? we need TCO numbers for the execs.
[05:03] Alex: we'll update the pilot sheet with estimated cost reduction and worst-case risk. preliminary is 12-15% token cost savings; but with extra infra egress it's net ~10% in our test. we'll quantify for your actual traffic mix.
[05:17] Sara: any known incompatibilities with our private deployment? we're on a VPC with strict outbound rules.
[05:23] Alex: Redwood Private supports VPC peering and on-prem connectors. for this pilot we requested temporary testing endpoints; in long term we can deploy Redwood control-plane connectors inside your VPC.
[05:34] Lina: legal asked about data residency, do you store any cache outside region?
[05:38] Jordan: policy is region-bound unless configured otherwise. we'll put documentation link in the follow-up.
[05:44] Tom: small note — in our load tests we saw a surge pattern at 9:12am that makes warmup harder. might be correlated to scheduled batch jobs. we'll try to shift schedule.
[05:55] Priya: thanks, that burst pattern explains some eviction thrashing. okay let me recap immediate changes we plan to push: improve token normalization, slight increase in coalesce window to 90s for certain routes, implement conditional longer TTL for templates routes, and add more observability for eviction traces.
[06:12] Alex: good. let's capture next steps: schedule the 2-hour steady-state run on 2027-04-08, send perf sheet by 4/4, bench script by 4/6, prompts by 4/5.
[06:22] Mike: that works. last question — any blockers we should know before the run?
[06:26] Priya: only permission and network access plus Sara's prompt set; otherwise engineers are ready.
[06:32] Alex: thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email and set the calendar invite for the 4/8 run.

End of transcript.

Notes: transcription includes some mis-hearings (e.g., 'prefetech' for prefetch, 'K-V' vs 'KV'); speaker labels are approximate.
